summary: Moses expresses doubts about his mission to the Lord, citing the people's disbelief and his own poor speaking skills (vv. 1, 10). The Lord gives Moses three miraculous signs to prove his authority and appoints Aaron as his spokesman (vv. 2-9, 14-16). Moses then begins his journey back to Egypt with his family, where he is instructed to confront Pharaoh and warn him of a plague on the firstborn (vv. 18-23). During the journey, the Lord seeks to kill Moses, but his wife Zipporah saves him by circumcising their son (vv. 24-26). Finally, Moses and Aaron meet, gather the Israelite elders, and perform the signs, leading the people to believe and worship (vv. 27-31).
setting: The chapter is set in Midian, where Moses has been living, and on the journey from Midian to Egypt (vv. 1, 19-20). Moses had fled Egypt many years prior and was working as a shepherd (Exodus 2:15, 21-22). The wider situation is that the Israelites are enslaved in Egypt, and the Lord is preparing Moses to lead them out (Exodus 3:7-10).

events.what: Moses tells the Lord that the Israelites will not believe him.
The Lord gives Moses a sign: his rod turns into a serpent and back again, so the people may believe.
The Lord gives Moses a second sign: his hand becomes leprous and then healed, for the people to believe.
The Lord gives Moses a third sign: water from the river will turn to blood on dry land, if the people do not believe the first two signs.
Moses tells the Lord he is not a good speaker, being slow of speech.
The Lord becomes angry and appoints Aaron, Moses's brother, to speak for Moses, because Moses asked for someone else to be sent.
Moses gets permission from Jethro to return to Egypt.
The Lord tells Moses to return to Egypt because those who sought his life are dead.
The Lord instructs Moses to perform wonders before Pharaoh and warns that He will harden Pharaoh's heart, leading to the death of Pharaoh's firstborn if he refuses to let Israel go.
The Lord seeks to kill Moses during his journey, but Zipporah circumcises their son, and the Lord lets Moses go.
Moses and Aaron meet, gather the elders of Israel, and Aaron speaks to the people and performs the signs.
The people believe, bow their heads, and worship the Lord after seeing the signs and hearing that the Lord had visited them.

people.name: Moses
people.role: The central figure, chosen by the Lord to lead the Israelites, who expresses doubts about his ability to speak and be believed.

people.name: The Lord
people.role: The divine entity who commissions Moses, gives him signs, appoints Aaron, and threatens Pharaoh.

people.name: Israelites
people.role: The people enslaved in Egypt whom Moses is sent to deliver.

people.name: Aaron
people.role: Moses's brother, appointed by the Lord to be Moses's spokesman to the people and Pharaoh.

people.name: Jethro
people.role: Moses's father-in-law, who gives Moses permission to return to Egypt.

people.name: Zipporah
people.role: Moses's wife, who circumcises her son to save Moses's life.

people.name: Moses's sons
people.role: Unnamed, one of whom is circumcised by Zipporah.

people.name: Pharaoh
people.role: The ruler of Egypt, whom Moses is commanded to confront.

people.name: Elders of the children of Israel
people.role: Representatives of the Israelite people who hear Moses and Aaron.

terms.meaning: A staff or stick, often used by shepherds for guidance and defense (v. 2). In this context, it becomes an instrument for performing signs (v. 17).
A skin condition, described here as white like snow, which was considered a severe impurity in ancient Israel (v. 6).
Skilled at speaking, able to express oneself clearly and persuasively (v. 10). Moses claims he is not eloquent.
A region east of the Gulf of Aqaba, where Moses lived after fleeing Egypt (v. 19).
The cutting off of the foreskin of the male penis, a ritual practice among some ancient peoples, including the Israelites (v. 25).

A phrase used by Zipporah after circumcising her son, whose exact meaning is debated by scholars (vv. 25-26). Some interpret it as 'husband of blood' or 'bridegroom of blood,' possibly referring to the covenant sealed by blood.

readings.view: Scholars often note the presence of different literary traditions (J, E, P) within the Pentateuch, suggesting that the account of the Lord seeking to kill Moses (vv. 24-26) might be a fragment from an older, distinct tradition incorporated into the larger narrative. They also examine the cultural context of the signs and the role of the rod.

Many Jewish commentators emphasize Moses's humility and reluctance, seeing it as a sign of true leadership, and highlight the importance of the covenant of circumcision as a life-saving act (vv. 10, 24-26). The appointment of Aaron is seen as a consequence of Moses's repeated hesitation.

Some Christian readings focus on the Lord's power to use imperfect instruments (Moses's speech impediment) and the foreshadowing of divine judgment against Pharaoh (vv. 11-12, 21-23). The circumcision incident is sometimes interpreted in light of the New Testament's emphasis on spiritual circumcision over physical.

In Islamic tradition, Moses (Musa) is a revered prophet. The account of his call and the signs he performs are generally accepted as demonstrations of God's power and Moses's prophetic authority, though the specific details of the circumcision incident are not typically emphasized in the Quranic narrative.

oftenQuoted.ref: v. 11 "Who hath made man's mouth? or who maketh the dumb, or deaf, or the seeing, or the blind? have not I the Lord?"
oftenQuoted.caution: This verse is often quoted to emphasize the Lord's sovereignty over human abilities and disabilities. However, in its context, it is the Lord's direct response to Moses's complaint about being 'slow of speech' (v. 10), reassuring Moses that the Lord will enable him to speak effectively for his mission (v. 12).

oftenQuoted.ref: v. 21 "but I will harden his heart, that he shall not let the people go."
oftenQuoted.caution: This phrase is often quoted to discuss divine sovereignty and human free will. In its context, the Lord is telling Moses that despite the wonders he will perform, Pharaoh's heart will be hardened, leading to a prolonged struggle and ultimately the death of Pharaoh's firstborn (vv. 22-23).

oftenQuoted.ref: v. 23 "I will slay thy son, even thy firstborn."
oftenQuoted.caution: This verse is often quoted as a direct threat of divine judgment. In its context, it is the Lord's instruction to Moses on what to tell Pharaoh as a warning, establishing the stakes for Pharaoh's refusal to release the Israelites, whom the Lord calls 'my son, my firstborn' (v. 22).
